active-directory-certificate-services.desc: Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) is a Windows Server role for issuing and managing PKI certificates, reportedly adding ML-DSA support for post-quantum certificates in 2026.

faq.a: AD CS is a Windows Server role for issuing and managing PKI certificates. It lets an organization operate its own certificate infrastructure.
faq.q: What is Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS)?

faq.a: According to the episode, AD CS added ML-DSA support for post-quantum certificates in 2026. No further technical details are given in the available information.
faq.q: Does AD CS support post-quantum certificates?

faq.a: Microsoft publishes an overview of Active Directory Certificate Services in its Windows Server documentation on Microsoft Learn, under the identity section for AD CS.
faq.q: Where can I find official documentation for AD CS?

active-directory-certificate-services.long:
Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) is a Windows Server role used to issue and manage certificates as part of a public key infrastructure (PKI). Organizations use such a role to run their own certification authority and to provide certificates for identity, authentication and related security scenarios inside a Windows environment.

According to the episode that references it, AD CS added support for ML-DSA, a post-quantum signature algorithm, in 2026. This would allow certificates based on post-quantum cryptography to be issued from the role. The available information on this change is limited to that statement, so details such as supported versions, configuration steps or rollout timing are not covered here.

Microsoft provides an overview of the role in its Windows Server documentation under the identity section for AD CS. That documentation is the reference point for the role's general purpose and capabilities.

On M365.FM, AD CS appears in the context of a discussion of post-quantum certificate support. No specific episode titles or related topic links are listed for this entity at this time.

activity-explorer.desc: Activity explorer is a Microsoft Purview tool that shows a historical view of activities on labeled content, including label changes and DLP events, based on the unified audit log.

faq.a: Activity explorer is a Microsoft Purview tool that gives a historical view of activities on labeled content. It is based on the unified audit log.
faq.q: What is Activity explorer in Microsoft Purview?

faq.a: It shows activities such as labels being applied, changed or removed, as well as DLP events.
faq.q: What kinds of activities does Activity explorer show?

faq.a: The data is based on the unified audit log, which is the source for the historical activity view the tool presents.
faq.q: Where does the data in Activity explorer come from?

activity-explorer.long:
Activity explorer is a tool in Microsoft Purview that provides a historical view of activities on labeled content. It draws on the unified audit log and surfaces events such as sensitivity labels being applied, changed or removed, as well as data loss prevention (DLP) events.

In practice, the tool is used to review how labels and protection policies are actually behaving across an organization. Administrators can look at past activity on labeled content to understand how information protection settings are used and to see where DLP policies have been triggered. This makes it a reporting and review aid alongside the configuration work done in Microsoft Purview Information Protection and Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention.

On M365.FM, Activity explorer comes up in episodes covering Microsoft Purview and related protection topics. These include Configure Microsoft 365 DLP Policies in Purview, Microsoft Purview Information Protection - Simply Explained, Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention (DLP) - Simply Explained, and Microsoft Purview vs Azure Information Protection. It is also mentioned in the discussion Protect Microsoft Copilot with Purview, DLP, and Insider Risk with Alan Cox [MVP], and in What Is Microsoft Intune Used For?.

Microsoft documents the tool in its Microsoft Purview data classification documentation on Microsoft Learn.

adaptive-card-designer.desc: Adaptive Cards Designer is a Microsoft web-based visual tool for authoring Adaptive Cards with drag-and-drop elements, sample-data previews and copyable JSON templates.

faq.a: Adaptive Cards Designer is a web-based visual tool from Microsoft for authoring Adaptive Cards. It offers drag-and-drop elements, previews with sample data and a copyable JSON template.
faq.q: What is Adaptive Cards Designer?

faq.a: It produces a JSON template for the card that has been designed. Users can copy this JSON for use in their own solutions.
faq.q: What does Adaptive Cards Designer produce as output?

faq.a: Microsoft documents the tool on Microsoft Learn, in the Adaptive Cards SDK section on the designer.
faq.q: Where is Adaptive Cards Designer documented?

adaptive-card-designer.long:
Adaptive Cards Designer is a web-based visual tool from Microsoft for authoring Adaptive Cards. Instead of writing card JSON by hand, authors build a card on a design surface and can see how it looks as they work.

The Designer lets users drag and drop elements onto a card, preview the card with sample data, and copy the resulting JSON template. This makes it useful for creating the card payloads that applications and bots send to their users, and for checking how a template renders with example values before it is used elsewhere.

Official documentation for the Adaptive Cards Designer is available on Microsoft Learn, in the Adaptive Cards SDK section.

On M365.FM, the Adaptive Cards Designer appears in connection with the episode "Build Microsoft Teams Apps with Bots, Tabs, and Extensions" (published 2025-08-12), which covers building apps for Microsoft Teams.

adaptive-card-extensions.desc: Adaptive Card Extensions (ACEs) are SharePoint Framework components that use Adaptive Cards to render cards on Viva Connections dashboards, on desktop and mobile.

faq.a: Adaptive Card Extensions (ACEs) are SharePoint Framework (SPFx) components that use Adaptive Cards to render cards on Viva Connections dashboards. They work in both the desktop and mobile experience.
faq.q: What are Adaptive Card Extensions (ACEs)?

faq.a: ACEs render as cards on Viva Connections dashboards, in the desktop and mobile experience. A card can optionally have a quick view.
faq.q: Where do ACEs appear?

faq.a: The episode "Customize Microsoft Viva Connections Dashboards" from 2025-08-13 covers Adaptive Card Extensions (ACEs) in the context of customizing Viva Connections dashboards.
faq.q: Which M365.FM episode covers ACEs?

adaptive-card-extensions.long:
Adaptive Card Extensions (ACEs) are SharePoint Framework (SPFx) components that use Adaptive Cards to render cards on Viva Connections dashboards. They are designed to display on both the desktop and the mobile experience of Viva Connections, and a card can optionally include a quick view.

In practice, ACEs are used to extend a Viva Connections dashboard with custom cards built by developers. Because they are based on SPFx, they follow the same development model as other SharePoint Framework components, while the Adaptive Card format defines how the card content is rendered. The optional quick view provides an additional view associated with a card.

On M365.FM, Adaptive Card Extensions (ACEs) appear in the episode "Customize Microsoft Viva Connections Dashboards" (published 2025-08-13), which covers customizing Viva Connections dashboards.

adaptive-cards.desc: Adaptive Cards are platform-agnostic UI snippets written in JSON that host apps like Microsoft Teams, Outlook and Copilot Studio render as native interface elements.

faq.a: Adaptive Cards are platform-agnostic UI snippets written in JSON. Host apps such as Microsoft Teams, Outlook and Copilot Studio render them as native UI.
faq.q: What are Adaptive Cards?

faq.a: Power Automate uses Adaptive Cards for interactive approval and notification messages, so recipients can respond directly within the message.
faq.q: How does Power Automate use Adaptive Cards?

faq.a: Episodes include "Build Actionable Teams Notifications with Adaptive Cards" and "Build Interactive Microsoft Teams Adaptive Cards", as well as episodes on Teams apps, bots and Jira Service Management integration.
faq.q: Which M365.FM episodes cover Adaptive Cards?

adaptive-cards.long:
Adaptive Cards are platform-agnostic UI snippets authored in JSON. A host application receives the card definition and renders it as native UI, so the same card payload can appear in different Microsoft products. Microsoft Teams, Outlook and Copilot Studio are named as host apps that render Adaptive Cards.

In practice, Adaptive Cards are used to present structured, interactive content inside messages and conversations. Power Automate uses them for interactive approval and notification messages, which allows a person to respond to a request directly from the message instead of opening a separate application. Official documentation for the format is published on Microsoft Learn.

On M365.FM, Adaptive Cards appear in several episodes focused on Microsoft Teams development and notifications. These include "Build Actionable Teams Notifications with Adaptive Cards" and "Build Interactive Microsoft Teams Adaptive Cards". They also come up in episodes on app development and integration, such as "Build Microsoft Teams Apps with Bots, Tabs, and Extensions", "Build Microsoft Teams Meeting Apps and Bots" and "Integrate Jira Service Management with Microsoft Teams". The episode "Reduce Microsoft 365 Notification Overload and Protect Focus" covers notification handling in Microsoft 365, a context in which card-based messages are relevant.

advanced-connector-policies.desc: Advanced connector policies (ACP) are a Power Platform governance capability for controlling which connectors, including MCP servers, may be used in an environment.

faq.a: Advanced connector policies are a Power Platform governance capability for controlling which connectors, including MCP servers, may be used in an environment.
faq.q: What are Advanced connector policies (ACP)?

faq.a: They complement classic data loss prevention (DLP) policies. They are described as an addition to DLP rather than a replacement for it.
faq.q: How do Advanced connector policies relate to DLP policies?

faq.a: Yes. MCP servers are included among the connectors whose use in an environment can be controlled with advanced connector policies.
faq.q: Do Advanced connector policies cover MCP servers?

advanced-connector-policies.long:
Advanced connector policies (ACP) are a Power Platform governance capability used to control which connectors may be used in an environment. The scope includes MCP servers, which are treated as connectors that can be allowed or restricted under these policies.

ACP complement classic data loss prevention (DLP) policies rather than replacing them. Classic DLP policies are the established mechanism for governing connector usage in Power Platform, and advanced connector policies add a further layer of control on top of that approach. Administrators responsible for Power Platform governance would use this capability when they need finer or additional control over connector availability in a given environment.

The available information about Advanced connector policies (ACP) is limited. No specific configuration steps, licensing details, supported connector types beyond MCP servers, or release information are stated here, so those points are not covered. For authoritative details, the official Microsoft documentation for Power Platform governance is the appropriate reference.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic.

agent-feed.desc: Agent feed (Copilot Studio) is a supervision view for autonomous Copilot Studio agents, showing which actions were completed, needed user input, or failed.

faq.a: It is a supervision view for autonomous Copilot Studio agents. It lets people review what an agent has done and step in where needed.
faq.q: What is the Agent feed in Copilot Studio?

faq.a: It shows which actions an agent completed autonomously, which required user input, and which failed.
faq.q: What information does the Agent feed show?

faq.a: It supports human oversight of autonomous agents, so reviewers can check outcomes and intervene when an action needs input or has failed.
faq.q: Why is the Agent feed useful?

agent-feed.long:
Agent feed (Copilot Studio) is a supervision view for autonomous agents built in Copilot Studio. It gives people a place to follow what an agent has done on its own, so that its work can be reviewed rather than taken on trust.

The view sorts an agent's activity by outcome. It shows which actions the agent completed autonomously, which actions required input from a user, and which actions failed. This separation helps reviewers see where an agent worked without help, where it stopped to ask a human, and where something went wrong.

The main purpose of the Agent feed is human oversight. By surfacing completed, blocked and failed actions in one view, it allows people to check the agent's results and to intervene when an action needs attention, for example when a user response is outstanding or an action did not succeed.

The available facts describe the Agent feed only at this level. No further details about configuration, licensing, availability or related products are stated here, so this page does not go beyond that description. No M365.FM episodes are linked to this topic yet.

faq.a: No episodes are linked to this entry at the moment. The page will be updated if relevant episodes are added.

Agent flows (Copilot Studio) is listed as a product entry within the Microsoft ecosystem, associated with Copilot Studio. The name suggests a feature tied to building or orchestrating agents in that environment.

The information currently available to M365.FM for this entry is limited to its name and its connection to Copilot Studio.
